title: Inside a Story
theme: Literary analysis: how plots are built and why characters act
objectives: I can name the main parts of a plot: exposition, complication, crisis, climax, and the ending.
I can explain a character's motivation and use evidence from the text to support it.
I can describe how an author builds tension and how readers anticipate what will happen.
I can write about a story using exact words instead of 'the exciting part' or 'the problem'.
rationale: Students need the terms for plot structure (exposition, complication, crisis, climax) and the words for pressure and turning points (tension, anticipate, pivotal, culminate) before they can analyze how a story is built. The unit pairs two character words (protagonist, motivation) with the plot sequence so that students can explain not only what happens but why a character acts and how each event leads to the next. Every later literary analysis in the year, including theme, point of view, and poetry, depends on this shared vocabulary.

words.def: The main character in a story, whose struggles the plot follows.
words.ex: The protagonist of the novel is a twelve-year-old girl who trains a stray dog.
words.ex2: In many fables, the protagonist is a clever animal that outwits a stronger one.
words.nonExample: A character who appears for one page and never returns is not the protagonist.

apps.academic: To find the protagonist, ask whose problem drives the plot.
apps.spoken: Who is the protagonist in the book you are reading?
apps.writing: Use protagonist for the central character, and say what that character wants.

cloze.s: The ___ of the story is Ana, a young sailor who must cross the bay in a storm.

cloze2.s: Because the story follows Marcus through every challenge, he is clearly its ___.

misuse.s: The protagonist is a minor character who appears once in the middle and never again.
misuse.why: The protagonist is the main character, not a minor one who appears once.

visual.alt: An open book with a hero figure rising from the pages.

words.def: The moment of greatest tension or action in a story, when the main problem comes to a head.
words.ex: The climax of the movie is the race across the frozen lake.
words.ex2: At the climax, the hero finally faces the storm that has been building all story long.
words.nonExample: The opening scene that introduces the characters is not the climax.

apps.academic: On a plot diagram, the climax is the highest point before the story starts to wind down.
apps.spoken: That chapter was the climax of the whole book.
apps.writing: Use climax for the peak of the plot, not for the end of the story.

cloze.s: In the ___ of the story, the boat tilted on a huge wave and Ana had to decide in seconds.

cloze2.s: The author slows down the writing at the ___, so each second of the final fight feels long.

misuse.s: The climax is the quiet first scene where the setting is described.
misuse.why: The climax is the moment of greatest tension, not a quiet opening scene.

visual.alt: A mountain peak shaped like a rising plot line.

words.def: The part of a story that introduces the characters, the setting, and the background.
words.ex: The exposition tells us that the story takes place in a fishing village long ago.
words.ex2: Some authors put the exposition in the first paragraph, and others reveal it slowly.
words.nonExample: A sudden fight in the middle of the story is not part of the exposition.

apps.academic: In your summary, describe the exposition before you describe the conflict.
apps.spoken: The exposition was a little slow, but it helped me understand the characters.
apps.writing: Use exposition for the background readers need at the start of a story.

cloze.s: The ___ introduced the main characters and showed the quiet harbor where the story begins.

cloze2.s: By the end of the ___, readers know where the story takes place and what the hero wants.

misuse.s: The exposition comes at the very end, where the characters say goodbye.
misuse.why: The exposition introduces the characters and setting at the beginning, not at the end.

visual.alt: A village scene on the first page of a book.

words.def: A feeling of worry or excitement that grows when you do not know what will happen.

senses.def: The pulling force that stretches a rope or wire tight.
senses.example: The tension on the kite string made it hum in the wind.

words.ex: The tension in the room rose as the judge opened the envelope.
words.ex2: The author builds tension by describing the footsteps getting closer.
words.nonExample: A relaxed picnic with nothing at stake has no tension.

apps.academic: Authors create tension with short sentences and unanswered questions.
apps.spoken: You could feel the tension in the gym before the final shot.
apps.writing: Use tension for the worry or suspense a reader feels, and name what causes it.

cloze.s: Hearing footsteps behind her in the empty hallway, Mira felt the ___ grow with every step.

cloze2.s: The short, quick sentences added ___ to the scene, so readers turned the page fast.

misuse.s: The tension in the story disappeared whenever the hero faced danger, and readers worried less.
misuse.why: Tension is worry or suspense that grows with danger; it does not disappear when danger appears.

visual.alt: A nervous face beside an hourglass.

words.def: To expect something and get ready for it, or to guess what will happen next.
words.ex: The coach anticipated that the other team would try a long pass.
words.ex2: Readers anticipate trouble when the sky in a story suddenly grows dark.
words.nonExample: Being completely surprised by something does not mean you anticipated it.

apps.academic: Good readers anticipate what will happen next and then check their prediction.
apps.spoken: I anticipated that traffic would be bad, so I left early.
apps.writing: Use anticipate for expecting something and preparing for it.

cloze.s: Because the forecast showed heavy snow, the town ___ long delays and sent the plows out early.

cloze2.s: A good chess player can ___ several moves ahead of the opponent.

misuse.s: She anticipated the surprise party by being shocked and having no idea.
misuse.why: To anticipate is to expect something; being shocked with no idea means she did not expect it.

words.def: A moment of serious trouble or danger when something important must be decided.
words.ex: The ship's engine failure created a crisis for everyone on board.
words.ex2: At the story's crisis, the hero must choose between two hard options.
words.nonExample: A small mistake that is easy to fix is not a crisis.

apps.academic: In a plot, the crisis is the point where the character faces the hardest choice.
apps.spoken: We had a crisis when the power went out during the show.
apps.writing: Use crisis for a moment of serious danger or choice, not for any small problem.

cloze.s: When the dam began to leak, the town faced a ___ and had to act within the hour.

cloze2.s: The story reaches a ___ when Ana must choose between saving the boat and saving the cargo.

misuse.s: Spilling one drop of water on the table was a crisis that required an emergency evacuation.
misuse.why: A crisis is a serious emergency; one drop of water is not one.

visual.alt: A flashing siren beside a rising wave.

words.def: Extremely important because everything after it depends on it, like a turning point.
words.ex: The pivotal scene shows Ana deciding to turn the boat back toward the island.
words.ex2: Winning the first round was pivotal for the team, because it gave them the confidence to win the rest.
words.nonExample: A detail that could be removed without changing the story is not pivotal.

apps.academic: Historians identify pivotal events that changed what happened next.
apps.spoken: That was a pivotal moment in my year.
apps.writing: Use pivotal for a moment that changes the direction of what follows.

cloze.s: The ___ moment came when the detective found the key under the stage and the whole mystery changed.

cloze2.s: The vote was ___ because it decided whether the club would continue or close.

misuse.s: The pivotal event was so unimportant that nothing changed afterward.
misuse.why: A pivotal event is extremely important and changes what follows.

visual.alt: A branching arrow beside a compass.

words.frame: A pivotal moment is one that ___.

words.def: To reach a final, highest point after a series of events.
words.ex: Weeks of practice culminated in a flawless performance at the recital.
words.ex2: The long conflict between the two families culminated in a dramatic confrontation at the fair.
words.nonExample: A story that stops in the middle does not culminate.

apps.academic: A story's rising action culminates in the climax.
apps.spoken: The week culminated in the school play.
apps.writing: Use culminate for the final peak of a chain of events.

cloze.s: Months of training for the race will ___ in one afternoon on the track.

cloze2.s: The series of small arguments between the friends ___ in a loud fight at the party.

misuse.s: The movie culminated at the very beginning, before any of the events occurred.
misuse.why: To culminate is to reach a peak after events; a beginning is not a peak.

visual.alt: A flag planted at the summit of a mountain.

words.def: A new problem that makes a situation more difficult.
words.ex: The first complication in the story is a broken bridge on the road to town.
words.ex2: A late bus was a complication for the field trip, since the museum had a strict schedule.
words.nonExample: A plan that goes exactly as expected has no complications.

apps.academic: In a plot, each complication adds a new obstacle for the main character.
apps.spoken: There's one complication: we only have one car.
apps.writing: Use complication for a new obstacle that changes the plan.

cloze.s: Rain was an unexpected ___ for the picnic, so the family had to move the table indoors.

cloze2.s: The story's first ___ appears when the hero loses the map the night before the journey.

misuse.s: The complication made the problem simpler and solved the whole plot at once.
misuse.why: A complication makes a situation harder, not simpler.

visual.alt: A tangle of yarn in front of a road barrier.

words.def: The reason a person wants to do something; what pushes a character to act.
words.ex: The hero's motivation is to protect her younger brother.
words.ex2: A strong motivation, like wanting to see her family, kept the hiker walking through the night.
words.nonExample: Knowing what a character looks like tells you nothing about the character's motivation.

apps.academic: To analyze a character, ask what the character's motivation is and how it changes.
apps.spoken: I'm having trouble finding the motivation to start my homework.
apps.writing: Use motivation for the reason behind an action, and support it with evidence.

cloze.s: Ana's ___ for crossing the bay is simple: she wants to prove that she is ready to captain a ferry.

cloze2.s: The story explains the villain's ___ early, so readers understand why he wants the treasure.

misuse.s: A character's motivation is the color of her coat and the name of her street.
misuse.why: Motivation is the reason a character acts, not a detail of appearance or address.

passage.title: Plot Talk in Room 12
paras: On Thursday, Mr. Alvarez's class discussed "The Last Ferry," a short story they had all read. He drew a plot diagram on the board and asked, "Where does the exposition end?" Imani raised her hand. "The exposition is the beginning, where we meet the protagonist, Ana, and learn that she lives on a small island and wants to be a ferry captain."

"Good," said Mr. Alvarez. "What is Ana's motivation?" "She wants to prove she is ready," said Imani. "That is why she volunteers to carry a message to the mainland, even though a storm is coming." Theo added, "The first complication is that the engine fails halfway across, so her simple plan becomes a struggle."

"Now look at the tension," said Mr. Alvarez. "How does the author build it?" Maya answered, "With small clues. The sky darkens and the gulls fly toward land, so readers anticipate trouble before it happens." Mr. Alvarez nodded. "Exactly. Good writers let you sense what is coming."

"What is the crisis?" he asked. Theo said, "Waves push the boat toward the rocks, and Ana has to choose between saving the message and saving the boat." "That choice is pivotal," Imani said, "because everything after it depends on what she decides." "And the climax?" asked Mr. Alvarez. "The moment of greatest tension," said Maya. "Ana lets the heavy bag slide overboard and steers away from the rocks."

"So where does the story culminate?" Mr. Alvarez asked. "At the dock," Imani said, "where Ana arrives safely and realizes that being a captain means making hard choices." Mr. Alvarez smiled. "Notice that none of this is random. Each event grows from the one before it, and that is how a plot is built."

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "exposition" most nearly means
choices: the part that introduces the characters and setting
the final scene of the story
the moment of greatest danger
the title and the author's name
qs.why: Imani describes the exposition as the beginning, where readers meet Ana and learn about her island and her goal.

qs.q: Why does Ana volunteer to carry the message even though a storm is coming?
choices: She does not know that a storm is coming.
She was ordered to by the ferry captain.
She wants to leave the island forever.
She wants to prove that she is ready to be a captain.
qs.why: Imani says Ana's motivation is to prove she is ready, which explains why she takes a risk.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the author builds tension with small clues?
choices: Ana lives on a small island.
The sky darkens and the gulls fly toward land.
The story is read by the whole class.
Ana arrives safely at the dock.
qs.why: The darkening sky and the gulls hint at danger before it happens, which makes readers anticipate trouble.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "pivotal" most nearly means
choices: slow and quiet
easy to forget
extremely important because what follows depends on it
silly and unrealistic
qs.why: Imani explains that everything after the choice depends on what Ana decides, which makes the moment a turning point.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: A story's ending is always happy.
Ferry captains must never carry messages.
Storms are the best way to start a story.
A plot is built from connected events that move from an introduction to a peak and then an ending.
qs.why: Mr. Alvarez summarizes that each event grows from the one before it, which is how a plot is built.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for analyzing how plots are built and why characters act, read a classroom conversation about a short story, and practice naming each part of a plot with evidence.

notes.va.protagonist.n: The protagonist is the center of the story, not necessarily a hero or a good person. Ask students what the protagonist wants and what stands in the way. The opposite is the antagonist, the force or character working against the protagonist.
notes.va.climax.n: Students often say the climax is the end. It is the peak of tension, usually near the end, but a falling action and a resolution can follow. Use a plot diagram to show it.
notes.va.exposition.n: Exposition is usually early, but authors can add background later. Have students find the exposition in a short story and underline the setting, the characters, and the problem to come.
notes.va.tension.n: Tension is a feeling that the author creates on purpose. Ask which details create it (sound, short sentences, ticking time). The rope sense (a pulling force) shows the same idea: something stretched tight and ready to snap.
notes.va.anticipate.v: Anticipate is stronger than guess: it involves preparing or expecting with a reason. Link to prediction in reading. Students sometimes confuse it with participate; the first syllables sound alike.
notes.va.crisis.n: The plural is crises (KRY-seez). In some plot diagrams the crisis comes just before the climax; in others it is part of the rising action. Name your model and keep it consistent. Do not use crisis for every problem.
notes.va.pivotal.adj: Pivotal comes from pivot, the point on which something turns. Ask which scene could not be removed without changing the ending. Distinguish pivotal (changes direction) from important (matters).
notes.va.culminate.v: Culminate is a verb for reaching a peak after a build-up; it always needs something that came before. Link to climax: events culminate in a climax. Students may think it only means end; it means the high point that ends a build-up.
notes.va.complication.n: A complication is a new problem that arrives after the story has started; it is part of the rising action. A plot can have several. Do not confuse it with the main conflict.
notes.va.motivation.n: Motivation is the why behind an action. Ask for evidence: what does the character say, do, or think that shows it? A character can have more than one motivation, and they can conflict.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'In the passage, Imani says Ana's motivation is to prove she is ready, and that explains why she volunteers in a storm. The engine failing is a complication because it makes her plan harder. The choice between the message and the boat is the crisis, and the moment she lets the bag go is the climax. I can use the words to explain each step.'
discuss: Can a story have more than one complication? What does each add?
How is the crisis different from the climax in a story you know?
misconceptions: The climax is the end of the story.
The protagonist is always a good person.
Exposition is only the first sentence.
Crisis and climax mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Draw a plot diagram for a short story and label each part using words from the unit.
Rewrite the story's exposition from the point of view of a different character and discuss how it changes the tension.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit impulsive and reluctant from unit 1 to describe protagonists, and trigger and outcome from unit 8 to connect plot events: ask what triggered the crisis and what was the outcome. Check recall at two days and one week.

wida.oral: Partner A retells a favorite story in four sentences. Partner B names the protagonist, the complication, and the climax using the unit words.

needsReview: Literary terms: the plot model (exposition, complication, crisis, climax) follows a common classroom plot diagram, but sources differ on where the crisis falls relative to the climax; a literature reviewer should confirm the framing in the teacher notes.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: decisivo (pivotal; 'crucial' also possible), exposición (exposition, as a plot term it may also be 'planteamiento'), tensión, clímax, culminar.
Sense boundary: tension includes a short physical-force second sense; crisis teaches the plural crises.
Passage is fiction (the story 'The Last Ferry' is invented for this unit); no factual claims.
Word-family study parts (motive, tense) are family groupings, not word-part claims; no etymology is stated.
